analysis.tldr: When global prices for gold and silver drop due to rising inflation worries, buying wedding jewelry or precious metals becomes cheaper for you.
the_story: Gold prices fell by Rs 1,500 per 10 grams on the MCX (Multi Commodity Exchange, where metals and commodities are traded).
Silver prices plunged by Rs 7,000 per kilogram on the MCX.
The drop happened because rising oil prices caused inflation concerns, leading to expectations of higher interest rates for a longer time.
Investors are closely watching the US Federal Reserve (America's central bank), the US dollar, and geopolitical tensions for further market cues.
analysis.what_happened: Gold and silver prices dropped sharply on the commodity exchange because oil prices are going up. Higher oil prices push up general inflation (rising prices of goods and services), which makes people think interest rates will stay high for a longer time. When interest rates stay high, precious metals become less attractive compared to keeping cash or bonds that earn interest.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local market where, when the price of fuel goes up, people panic that everything else will get expensive and start hoarding cash instead of buying shiny ornaments, causing jewelers to lower their prices to attract buyers.
why_it_matters_india: Oil prices rise globally -> inflation concerns grow worldwide
Central banks keep interest rates higher for longer -> investors prefer cash and bonds over metals
MCX gold and silver prices drop -> local retail buyers and jewelers get metals at lower prices in India
Geopolitical tensions and US dollar movements are watched -> shifts global money flows affecting Indian markets

impacts.rationale: Prices dropped on the commodity exchange, which is good for retail buyers and people planning wedding purchases in India.
A sharp plunge on the exchange means cheaper silver for industrial users and retail investors.
Soaring oil prices push up everyday costs, which hurts ordinary households through expensive fuel and transport.

watch_next: US Federal Reserve meeting announcements on interest rates
analysis.caveats: Only the headline and limited article text were available, so the full depth of broader market impacts relies heavily on known financial reactions to oil price shifts.

events.headline: Rising Crude Oil Imports Reduce China’s Need to Draw from Stocks

items.title: Rising Crude Oil Imports Reduce China’s Need to Draw from Stocks
items.summary: China has relied on its huge crude oil inventories since the Iran war hiked oil prices to above $100 per barrel. The world’s biggest crude importer has drawn from its 1.3-billion-barrel stash for most of the months after March as it slashed imports amid soaring prices. The stock draws, and the reduced imports in the spring and summer, have even kept benchmark crude oil prices in check despite the major disruption to flows from the Middle East, as China’s crude supply management was one of the key buffers the market has had since the…

events.article_text:
Brent Hits $114 as Houthi Attacks Threaten Saudi Energy Infrastructure

What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,…

China has relied on its huge crude oil inventories since the Iran war hiked oil prices to above $100 per barrel. The world’s biggest crude importer has drawn from its 1.3-billion-barrel stash for most of the months after March as it slashed imports amid soaring prices.

The stock draws, and the reduced imports in the spring and summer, have even kept benchmark crude oil prices in check despite the major disruption to flows from the Middle East, as China’s crude supply management was one of the key buffers the market has had since the war began.

Now it’s the only buffer left, after the global oil oversupply at the start of the year was absorbed and stock draws elsewhere depleted crude and fuel inventories.

China had amassed an estimated up to 1.4 billion barrels of crude in commercial and strategic stockpiles before the Iran war. The huge cushion allowed it to slash imports when the Strait of Hormuz closed, and prices spiked.

Ever the opportunistic buyer, China withdrew from the spot market shortly after the Middle East crisis erupted, and by slashing this import demand, Beijing single-handedly offset part of the lost global supply.

China’s crude importing policy in the spring managed to keep international oil prices capped, as about 4 million barrels per day (bpd) of crude didn’t have to reach Chinese refiners in April, May, and June.

China slashed its total crude oil imports to a decade low in June, culminating three months of very low import levels amid high prices and constrained supply from the Middle East. Beijing could afford to dramatically reduce its crude buying, slashing import volumes in June by an estimated 4.4 million bpd compared to the 2025 average. Related: Rising Crude Oil Imports Reduce China’s Need to Draw from Stocks

In July, China likely added some 200,000 bpd to its crude reserves after imports rebounded but refinery runs stayed low.

This was the only month of the past five in which China was estimated to have added to its reserves.

The world’s biggest crude oil importer tapped its inventories again in August and September, with the draws last month at about 530,000 bpd, as estimated by Reuters columnist Clyde Russell based on official data about imports, refinery throughput, and domestic production.

Unlike the United States, China does not report inventories. Analysts are looking at overall supply (domestic production plus imports) and refinery processing rates to estimate how much crude is going into reserves and how much is being processed into fuels.

Last month, China’s crude supply from imports and domestic production was about 13.46 million bpd, while refineries processed 13.99 million bpd, per Russell’s calculations.

Despite the stock draws for most of this year, China is still estimated to have at least 1.2 billion barrels of crude oil in commercial and strategic inventories.

No one is really certain how much, but it’s certain that the huge stock buffer allows China to tweak its crude import policy depending on the oil prices at the time it is ordering and arranging crude cargoes.

Chinese crude imports in October are likely to rebound to above 10 million bpd—the highest level since March, according to data from Kpler cited by Reuters’ Russell.

This wouldn’t be surprising, considering that oil prices held at about $80 per barrel Brent for most of August, when the October-imported cargoes would have been purchased.

This year, $80 a barrel of oil is encouraging higher Chinese buying activity, especially as the Brent average so far this year is just shy of $95 per barrel, and prices have kept above $100 for more than a month now.

Increased oil flows from the Middle East, the August oil price of about $80 a barrel, and the resumption of Chinese fuel exports will boost China’s crude oil imports in October.

This would reduce the need to tap the huge inventories. China would rather keep these for the coming months, when imports could slow again after the oil price spikes in September and October.

At the end of September, Goldman Sachs said that China’s crude oil exports would rise only slightly in the fourth quarter from the third quarter if oil prices remain high. At $100 per barrel Brent and above, it is unlikely that China would materially raise imports in the near term, the bank’s analysts said.

Other analysts also concur that China is not expected to materially boost its crude oil imports through the end of the year as oil prices surged again and independent Chinese refiners struggle to procure cheaper supply amid the near-disappearance of Iranian barrels.

Analysts at FGE NexantECA and Energy Aspects have revised down their earlier projections of China’s crude oil imports in the fourth quarter by about 400,000 bpd. The analysts now expect China’s crude oil imports to be 9.2 million bpd-9.3 million bpd in the fourth quarter, well below last year’s average of 11.6 million bpd.

If oil prices remain above $100 per barrel and the conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt trade flows, China could tap more of its massive inventories and reduce imports again. Lower Chinese imports would be some relief to the global oil market reeling from depleted inventories, a diesel crunch, and record-high fuel prices.

analysis.tldr: When China buys more foreign oil instead of using its secret stockpiles, global oil supplies tighten, risking higher petrol and diesel prices in India.
the_story: China has relied on its 1.3-billion-barrel to 1.4-billion-barrel crude oil inventories since the Iran war pushed oil prices above $100 per barrel.
China slashed its total crude oil imports to a decade-low in June, cutting import volumes by an estimated 4.4 million barrels per day compared to the 2025 average.
Chinese crude imports in October are expected to rebound to over 10 million barrels per day because oil prices dropped to about $80 per barrel in August when those cargoes were bought.
Analysts like FGE NexantECA and Energy Aspects expect China's fourth-quarter imports to be 9.2 million to 9.3 million barrels per day, well below last year's 11.6 million average.
analysis.what_happened: China, the world's biggest buyer of crude oil, stopped buying as much from other countries when prices spiked due to the Iran war, choosing instead to drain its massive hidden emergency stockpiles. Now, because global oil prices dipped to around $80 a barrel in August, China is stepping up its foreign purchases for October, reducing its need to empty those reserves.
analysis.analogy: It is like a giant household with a huge basement full of stored food; when grocery prices spike, they stop shopping and eat what is in the basement. When prices dip slightly, they start buying groceries from the market again.
why_it_matters_india: China increases its foreign oil purchases for October shipments.
More global oil demand from China reduces the available buffer for the rest of the world.
Global crude oil prices face upward pressure if conflicts disrupt Middle Eastern flows further.
India, which imports most of its oil, faces higher import bills, which can weaken the rupee and raise domestic fuel and inflation pressures.

impacts.rationale: As China increases its imports and uses fewer stored reserves, global demand picks up, which is generally bad for energy importers like India.
Higher global oil prices force India to spend more dollars to buy fuel, which weakens the rupee — making imported goods more expensive for regular people.
Costlier crude oil makes transport and manufacturing pricier, driving up everyday consumer prices, which is bad for household budgets.
Rising international crude costs put upward pressure on domestic fuel prices at the pump, increasing travel and transport costs.

watch_next: Whether actual Chinese import volumes in October stay above 10 million barrels per day
Updates on Middle Eastern shipping routes and conflict developments affecting oil flows
analysis.caveats: If oil prices surge back above $100 per barrel, China could quickly halt foreign purchases again and go back to draining its massive stockpiles.

events.headline: Why the minutes of RBI's rate-setting committee meeting hint at a course correction

items.title: Why the minutes of RBI's rate-setting committee meeting hint at a course correction
items.summary: The stark change in the stance of members from the prior policy meeting in August suggests that the inflationary impact of the foreign currency non-resident (bank) deposits was underestimated. Such missteps can prove costly.

events.article_text:
The minutes of the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting held earlier this month were eagerly awaited for two reasons. One, for the first time in RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra’s term, the MPC voted for a hike in policy rates. Two, after a long time, the opinions of members differed on the policy stance.

While the reasons for the change in stance—from neutral to calibrated tightening—are not entirely clear, most MPC members seem to have realized that they misread the inflation outlook and the liquidity position at the last meeting in early August.

Both the governor and the deputy governor were far more sanguine about the inflation trajectory in August. They seem to have underestimated the impact of the enormous liquidity boost because of the deposits received under the foreign currency non-resident (bank), or FCNR-B, scheme.

In August, the governor argued that there were “limited signs of generalisation of inflation with core inflation remaining modest.” Inflation, he said, was “expected to taper from its peak in Q3.” There is no need for a “monetary response to curtail demand as of now,” he noted.

Two months down the line, his assessment seems to have changed completely. In the October meeting, he noted the “risks of demand side pressures in view of the growth in monetary and credit aggregates.”

The RBI deputy governor in charge of monetary policy also offered very different assessments. In the August meeting, Poonam Gupta argued that risks to inflation and growth are evenly poised. Growth could turn out better than expected while “inflation could be marginally lower,” she said.

In October, however, she argued that monetary tightening would be required to contain rising inflationary pressures, and maintain the credibility of India’s inflation-targeting framework.

Both officials blamed external factors for the worsening of the inflation outlook. However, the geopolitical factors impacting commodity prices haven’t seen much change between August and October.

The uncertainty on the oil front due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continued, as before, as did the likelihood of El Niño hitting our crop output adversely. The only big change involved the vast inflows of foreign funds (on account of FCNR-B deposits) pushing up domestic liquidity. This could have been, and should have been, foreseen.

The October rate hike seems partly an attempt to correct course and anchor inflationary expectations at a time when both inflation and bond yields are rising globally.

The narrowing spread between Indian and global bond yields may have contributed to the change in stance although just one MPC member referred to it explicitly. “Maintaining a certain gap between India and G7 interest rates is important for attracting debt capital flows,” Saugata Bhattacharya, who is an external member, noted. He also warned that the “broad monetary policy environment” in India may have become “too accommodative.”

The MPC minutes underline that the prospects of a rate cut are quite dim at this stage. The majority in the committee seem to have realized that they need to reaffirm their commitment to fighting inflation, and the change in stance seems to signal that intent. Both domestic and global conditions warrant a tight monetary policy. Policymakers can’t afford slip-ups.

analysis.tldr: The RBI (Reserve Bank of India, the central bank that manages the country's money) is shifting towards stricter borrowing rules to fight rising prices, making future loan cost cuts unlikely.
the_story: The RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC, the group that decides interest rates) voted for a policy rate hike for the first time under Governor Sanjay Malhotra, and members' opinions differed.
Members realized they misread the inflation outlook (how fast prices rise) and liquidity position (cash available in the banking system) from their early August meeting.
In August, officials underestimated the enormous cash boost from FCNR-B deposits (foreign currency deposits made by non-resident Indians) and thought inflation would ease.

By October, Governor Malhotra and Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta changed their assessments, warning of demand-side pressures and stating that monetary tightening (making money harder to borrow to cool down the economy) is needed.

External member Saugata Bhattacharya noted that maintaining a gap between Indian and G7 (group of seven major advanced economies) interest rates is important to attract debt capital flows (money coming from foreign lenders).
analysis.what_happened: The RBI's rate-setting committee changed its official stance from neutral to 'calibrated tightening' (a cautious move toward higher interest rates). Officials changed their minds because they realized they miscalculated the huge flood of cash coming into India from foreign currency bank deposits, which forced them to step in and try to control rising prices.
analysis.analogy: It is like a driver who thought the road ahead was flat and easy, only to realize they are speeding down a steep hill and suddenly need to press hard on the brakes.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI shifts its stance to fight inflation (rising prices of everyday goods).
To do this, the central bank signals that borrowing costs will stay high or go up, pushing down the chances of interest rate cuts.
Higher interest rates ripple through the economy, making loans for homes, cars, and businesses costlier.
At the same time, keeping Indian interest rates attractive compared to foreign countries helps keep foreign money invested in India.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: As the RBI tightens policy and fights inflation, government borrowing costs rise — which usually leads to costlier loans for everyone else, bad for borrowers.

impacts.target: Interest rates on consumer loans (home, car, personal)
impacts.rationale: With rate cuts off the table and a tighter policy stance, banks face higher costs and are less likely to lower loan EMIs (Equated Monthly Installments, fixed monthly loan payments) — bad for people wanting cheaper loans.
Stricter monetary policy and higher borrowing costs make it harder for companies to expand, which can put pressure on stock prices — generally disappointing for equity investors.
The entire point of the RBI's course correction is to pull down rising price pressures, which helps protect household purchasing power over time — good for consumers.

watch_next: Upcoming statements from RBI officials regarding banking liquidity
Global inflation and bond yield movements in the US and G7 nations
analysis.caveats: Unforeseen global shocks like sudden jumps in oil prices or weather events like El Niño disrupting crop outputs could force the RBI to shift course again.

events.headline: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes

items.title: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes
items.summary: Housing data deteriorated further in September, according to separate reports Tuesday.

events.article_text:
The Federal Reserve's inflation fight is running into a growing complication: The housing market is slumping even as broader price pressures persist.

Housing data deteriorated further in September, according to separate reports Tuesday, adding to an already complicated policy landscape for the central bank as it contemplates its next move on interest rates.

Things appear poised to get worse before they get better. If the Fed raises short-term rates as expected over the next several months, mortgage rates that are already at 7.43% could push even higher, putting a further damper on affordability. Higher home borrowing costs have coincided with a general rise in inflation and a housing shortage.

"The housing market is about to go into a deep sleep unless Washington can do a 180 on its policies and make the cost of a new home more affordable," wrote Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "It is not winter yet but housing is going into a deep freeze."

The National Association of Realtors reported that pending sales, a forward-looking index that measures home sales under agreement but not completed, hit an all-time low in records that stretch back to 2001. The index slid 7.3% for the month and was off 11.3% from a year ago. The Wall Street estimate was for a decline of just 0.4%.

Housing starts, another important metric when evaluating the state of the market, also posted a decline well outside already-muted expectations Tuesday.

Privately owned housing starts fell 5.2% on the month, against expectations for a decline of just 0.4%, while building permits were off 0.2%, against the Dow Jones consensus outlook for a 2% gain, according to Commerce Department data.

Moreover, single-family permits totaled just 845,000, down 4% from August and the lowest number since 2023.

"Market conditions weakened in September due to fast-rising mortgage rates," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. "Although job growth and income gains can support home purchases, housing affordability is more affected by changes in mortgage rates."

The rate for a 30-year mortgage was above 7% for most of September, ending the month around 7.6%, according to Mortgage News Daily. Five years ago, rates were closer to 3%, feeding into the Covid-era housing boom that saw an explosion in demand and, consequently, prices.

Outside of the pending sales number, home builder sentiment is at lows not seen in 14 years.

Under some conditions, Fed officials might respond to the housing weakness with easier monetary policy. Lower rates generally help spur demand by lowering borrowing costs.

But the Fed has a bigger fight on its hands in its effort to bring inflation under control. Readings last week on consumer and producer prices provided few signs of optimism, with wholesale final demand goods prices rising 2.6%, the fastest pace in a Bureau of Labor Statistics data series going back to December 2009.

Fed officials have said they are tracking the inflationary effects of the robust investment in artificial intelligence, which is driving up the cost of chips and electronics. At the same time, they believe that benefits from AI investment could offset weaker sectors of the economy such as housing.

However, conditions generally point to a housing market likely to weaken further before stabilizing, Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker said in a client note Monday.

"In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability—reignited by the recent rebound in mortgage rates—to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity," Walker wrote. "Sustained higher mortgage rates will continue to have their most pronounced impact on housing turnover, and the recent run-up in rates is likely to push existing home sales lower in the coming months."

Several data points tell the story: More than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the prevailing level, and 65% are 2 percentage points below. Goldman forecasts residential investment to decline 2.5%, 4% and 1%, respectively, over the coming three quarters, with a possibility for a steeper decline if mortgage rates don't fall.

The firm sees single-family starts of just 875,000 in 2027, little changed from this year, while existing sales are forecast at 3.9 million, also about the same as 2026 but notably 26% below pre-Covid 2019 levels. Walker attributed the middling levels as a product of the "lock-in" effect in which it's too expensive for current homeowners to move and take on higher borrowing costs while deteriorating affordability weighs on new construction.

"Housing activity has remained rangebound in recent years, capped on the upside by affordability headwinds and buffered on the downside by the longstanding housing shortage," Walker wrote. "In 2027, we expect the headwind from affordability to increasingly dominate, weighing further on activity."

Markets expect the Fed to hold benchmark rates steady when it meets next week. However, futures pricing implies a strong chance of a quarter-point hike in December and another in March 2027, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

One point of optimism comes from Yun, the NAR economist, who thinks the trend of mortgage costs running ahead of Fed hikes could mean that rates are topping out.

"Given that mortgage rates have already risen much more than the Federal Reserve's short-term interest rate hikes, mortgage rates could be topping out," he said. "Buyers and sellers may simply be holding back until mortgage rates move favorably."

analysis.tldr: If the US central bank keeps raising interest rates to fight inflation, it can make borrowing expensive there and trigger money to flow out of India, weakening the rupee.
the_story: The US Federal Reserve [the central bank of the United States that sets borrowing costs] faces a slumping US housing market while general price pressures (inflation) remain high.
US pending home sales hit an all-time low in September in records stretching back to 2001, dropping 7.3% for the month.
US privately owned housing starts fell 5.2% in September, and 30-year US mortgage rates sat above 7% for most of the month, ending around 7.6%.
Markets expect the US Fed to hold rates steady soon, but futures pricing implies a chance of hikes in December and March 2027.
Goldman Sachs forecasts US residential investment to decline over coming quarters and single-family starts to remain low due to high mortgage rates.
analysis.what_happened: The US housing market is slumping because home borrowing costs have surged, with 30-year mortgage rates climbing above 7%. At the same time, the US Federal Reserve is considering raising interest rates further because wider inflation remains a stubborn problem.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family trying to fix a kitchen fire while ignoring a leaking roof in the hallway—the central bank wants to stop overall inflation, but higher interest rates are freezing the housing market.
why_it_matters_india: The US Federal Reserve weighs more interest rate hikes to fight stubborn inflation.
Higher US interest rates make safe US investments more attractive to global capital.
Foreign investors (FIIs [big international institutional investors]) pull money out of emerging markets like India to chase better returns in the US.
Increased outflow of foreign money puts downward pressure on Indian financial markets and the rupee.

impacts.rationale: As US rates stay high, foreign money shifts to America, which weakens the rupee (each rupee buys fewer dollars) — making imported items like crude oil costlier for India.
If foreign investors pull money out of Indian shares due to rising US yields, local stock prices can face selling pressure, which is generally unsettling for local retail investors.

impacts.target: 10-year bond yield (interest India pays to borrow)
impacts.rationale: Global borrowing cost pressures can push Indian government bond yields higher, meaning the government pays more to borrow money.

watch_next: Statements from US Federal Reserve officials regarding future rate decisions
Trends in foreign investor buying or selling in Indian stock exchanges
analysis.caveats: If US inflation cools down faster than expected, the US Fed might drop plans for further rate hikes, easing pressure on global markets.

the_story: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman stated that the RBI (India's central bank that manages money and interest rates) may take extra steps to curb rupee volatility (bouncing up and down sharply).

analysis.what_happened: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman signalled that India's central bank will keep managing wild swings in our currency. analysis.analogy: It is like a parent gently holding a toddler's hand in a crowded market to stop them from running too fast in either direction, rather than forcing them to walk at one exact speed.
why_it_matters_india: The RBI steps in to sell dollars and restrict heavy betting against the local currency.
This sudden intervention cuts down wild fluctuations in the value of the rupee.
A steadier rupee helps prevent sudden spikes in the cost of imported items like crude oil.
Regular consumers see fewer sudden imported inflation shocks, keeping household budgets more predictable.

events.headline: To Import or Build? Southeast Asia’s Rolling Stock Dilemma

items.title: To Import or Build? Southeast Asia’s Rolling Stock Dilemma
items.summary: Some of the region's governments are moving toward manufacturing their own rolling stock – but this comes with trade-offs.

events.article_text:
Urban rail systems are growing fast across Southeast Asia. This is fueling demand for rolling stock – the train cars that actually carry millions of riders around town every day. The most common option is to import trainsets from established industry leaders in China, Japan, South Korea, or Europe. But some countries in Southeast are turning to domestic firms to meet their orders. This raises an obvious question: is this wise?

The trade-offs are clear enough. Importing trains from an established global brand like China’s CRRC means you are buying a proven product, with after-sales service and support that makes it easier to maintain the trains. Sometimes foreign firms also provide electronic systems like signalling, which makes system integration easier. For many rail providers, this is a fine deal. Metro and commuter rail systems in Bangkok and Manila rely mainly on imported rolling stock.

But some countries want more. They want to manufacture the rolling stock domestically because they believe it will generate local jobs, create long-term value, and develop important skills and technical expertise. If done well, it will allow domestic firms to grow and export their products. Indonesia is a prominent example of this strategy, with state-owned INKA producing rolling stock for the local market and for export.

INKA’s main customer is the state-owned railway company, KAI, with which it is currently in the process of merging. If you have ever traveled on an intercity train in Java it most likely was made by INKA. More recently, INKA supplied the rolling stock for the Greater Jakarta LRT and has been delivering new trainsets for Jakarta’s large, aging and very busy commuter rail system, the KRL.

INKA is a classic case of industrial policy. Rather than relying on foreign firms, the government requires KAI to procure some of its rolling stock from INKA and places restrictions on imports. This guarantees INKA a minimum level of orders while also protecting it from foreign competition, providing the train-maker some breathing room to develop industrial capabilities it might not otherwise be able to.

But here’s the catch. For such industrial policy to be effective, INKA needs to deliver the goods. It must deliver rolling stock on time and that meets basic quality standards. It must show evidence that it is making progress toward mastery of more complex technologies, skills and production capabilities. The government can bend the market to give a state-owned firm a leg up, but the firm needs to prove this intervention is worth it. Industrial policy fails when firms don’t make good use of the strategic advantage they have been given.

At the moment, INKA is struggling to deliver the goods. The train cars built for the LRT in 2023 were plagued with problems, including electrical and mechanical issues. Almost as soon as they went into service, many had to be pulled out and modified. The LRT project was run mainly by Indonesian SOEs, so the fact that it experienced growing pains was not necessarily evidence of policy failure. The key was that domestic firms, including INKA, learned from these mistakes and used them to improve.

In recent weeks, rolling stock made by INKA for Jakarta’s commuter rail system has been malfunctioning, throwing commutes into chaos. Doors are getting stuck open, forcing trains out of service. Seven cars were recalled after KAI raised concerns about structural weakness in the undercarriage. KAI is seeking special permission from the government to import used rolling stock from Japan to meet immediate operational needs while these issues are worked out. Public anger and scrutiny are rising.

Similar attempts by other home-grown firms in the region also have spotty records. In 2011, Malaysia’s Scomi won a nearly 500 million ringgit contract to supply trainsets for the Kuala Lumpur monorail. The rolling stock was delivered late, and faced performance and safety issues. The procurement became embroiled in legal disputes, and Scomi was eventually dissolved. So INKA is not alone in facing hurdles as it tries to expand its footprint. But if the government is to continue aiding such efforts, INKA needs to start delivering the goods.

This is especially true now that intra-ASEAN competition is intensifying. Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup just announced it was launching a joint venture with France’s Alstom to co-produce 200 trainsets for the Hanoi metro under a technology licensing agreement. This is a very large and ambitious project, which would represent a major step-up in capabilities for Vingroup and Vietnam’s domestic railway industry. Of course, Vingroup has a history of taking huge swings that don’t always pan out. So we will have to see.

Most urban rail systems in Southeast Asia simply import their trains, working with established manufacturers who can deliver a proven product and after-sales service and support. For some countries, domestic manufacturing is a more important goal and the state will intervene to give local firms a head-start. Ultimately, no amount of state support or industrial policy can cover up for production failings that leave commuters stranded with unreliable products. The trains must run, and local firms like INKA must deliver the goods. Otherwise, the whole logic of industrial policy comes flying off the rails.

analysis.tldr: Southeast Asian countries are struggling to build their own trains instead of importing them, serving as a reminder of the massive hurdles countries face when trying to build complex manufacturing industries at home.
the_story: Urban rail systems across Southeast Asia are growing fast, creating high demand for rolling stock (the train cars that carry passengers).

While countries like Thailand (implied by Bangkok) and the Philippines (Manila) mainly import proven trains from giants like China's CRRC, Japan, South Korea, or Europe, others like Indonesia and Malaysia have tried building them domestically.

Indonesia's state-owned train maker, INKA, has faced severe product failures, including electrical issues on the Greater Jakarta LRT in 2023 and recent commuter rail train breakdowns with stuck doors and structural undercarriage weaknesses.
Malaysia's home-grown firm Scomi won a 500 million ringgit contract in 2011 for Kuala Lumpur monorail trains, but faced delays, safety issues, legal disputes, and eventual company dissolution.
Intra-ASEAN competition is heating up as Vietnam's Vingroup partners with France's Alstom to co-produce 200 trainsets for the Hanoi metro.
analysis.what_happened: Southeast Asian nations face a dilemma between importing reliable, pre-made trains from global giants or using government protection and rules to force domestic companies to build trains themselves. While local manufacturing aims to create jobs and master complex technology, domestic firms like Indonesia's INKA are struggling with severe production, quality, and delivery issues.
analysis.analogy: It is like a family trying to build their own car in the garage from scratch to save local pride, instead of buying a reliable factory-made car—only to find the homemade engine keeps breaking down on the way to work.
why_it_matters_india: Southeast Asian manufacturing struggles highlight how difficult it is to shift from importing goods to successfully building complex heavy machinery domestically.

As India pushes its own 'Make in India' manufacturing initiatives for heavy transport and railways, it serves as a real-world example of the quality and execution hurdles state-backed domestic firms face.
Intense competition in Southeast Asia involves global giants from China, Japan, and Europe, keeping competitive pressure on global manufacturing supply chains.
Indian engineering and railway export aspirations must navigate these same global quality standards and stiff international competition.

impacts.rationale: Global manufacturing hiccups in emerging markets can occasionally sap broad sentiment toward emerging market equities, though the direct link to India is very weak.
Broader global trade shifts and emerging market currency pressures can have tiny psychological ripples on the rupee, but this news is hyper-local to Southeast Asia.

watch_next: Whether Indonesia's KAI is granted permission to import used trains from Japan
Progress on Vietnam's Vingroup and Alstom joint venture train production in Hanoi
analysis.caveats: This article focuses entirely on Southeast Asia, so any implications for Indian manufacturing are strictly lessons in industrial policy rather than direct economic impacts.

events.headline: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance

items.title: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance
items.summary: This photograph taken on September 6, 2026 shows a placard opposing data centers displayed on a water dispenser during the People's Convention on AI Data Centers event at Visakhapatnam in India's Andhra Pradesh state. Construction of a massive Google data centre in the Indian city of Visakhapatnam, often called Vizag, has been met with resistance from residents, who fear the impact on the environment and their lives. But the tech giant says its "gigawatt-scale" AI facility -- in southern Andhra Pradesh state, part of a $15 billion investment -- will use air cooling systems, and not water from

events.article_text:
After ChatGPT was released in November 2022, the tech industry was quick to herald the chatbot as the marker of a new wave of technological progress. As companies pushed to create more powerful AI models, the water demand of their ambitions took a while to become clear. In April 2023, a research paper out of the University of California estimated that training the large language model behind the initial version of ChatGPT had required 185,000 gallons of water. For every extended conversation someone had with the chatbot or every time they asked it to write an email, they were effectively pouring a bottle of water down the drain.

That statistic got a lot of play when it was released. It became an early warning sign of what was coming as companies pushed chatbots as a universal technology that could replace psychologists, educators, lawyers, and even people’s friends or partners.

As public concern grew, Google and OpenAI came out with their own figures. The companies suggested that querying one of their chatbots used mere drops of water. Independent researchers were not impressed, arguing the companies were taking a narrow view of the water use necessary to power and cool increasingly monstrous data centers. Those water demands can be quite significant too.

A hyperscale data center can suck up between 1 and 5 million gallons of water a day, comparable to the amount used by a city of 10,000 to 50,000 people — depending on the part of the world we’re talking about. Consider how these companies often cluster data centers together and it becomes obvious what a challenge it can be to supply them.

The water demands of individual data centers are also continuing to grow. It’s not just that they need more water for cooling as they become larger and contain more servers. The graphics processing units (GPUs) that power generative AI are much more resource-intensive than the chips and storage devices that traditionally filled data center racks. GPUs run harder and throw off more heat, meaning they also need more energy or water to keep them cool.

Data centers cannot just use any kind of water either; it has to be clean enough to ensure the equipment and pipes are not damaged. Tapping into public drinking water is both easier and cheaper than paying the cost of treatment themselves. That means data centers end up competing with communities over their potable water supply.

If we want to look at a part of the world where the issue of data center water use has taken center stage, there are few better countries to turn to than Chile. In October 2019, mass social demonstrations broke out across the country. One of the movement’s driving slogans was about water. It was poor timing for Google as it was fighting for approval and public support of its latest data center project, a $200 million data center project in Cerrillos, on the southwest side of Santiago.

The company made a pitch similar to the one residents in communities the world over have heard whenever a data center is proposed: that the facility would bring jobs and prosperity, and give the area a leg up on further tech investments. The reality was not so straightforward. Google’s new data center would bring a lot of short-term construction jobs but not much long-term employment. And it would need a lot of water — something Cerrillos did not have much of to spare.

Local residents were not as passive as the company had hoped. A group of concerned citizens established an organization called MOSACAT, which stands for Community Socio-Environmental Movement for Water and Land, and started poring over whatever information they could get their hands on to try to understand what the project would mean for them. “Usually these reports use quite technical language, and this is a working- class community where not many people are lawyers, for example, or experts on ecology,” explains Sebastián Lehuedé, a researcher at King’s College London who is from Chile and spent time in Cerrillos.

According to its own projections, the data center Google wanted to build in Cerrillos was poised to use 169 liters of water every single second. In just one day, the data center would consume as much water as all 80,000 residents of Cerrillos use for drinking in a year. To make matters worse, it wanted to draw that water from an underground aquifer that had been under a decree that restricted how much water could be removed since 2005. Just weeks before the project was rubber-stamped by the environmental authority, that decree had been upgraded to a complete prohibition on new extraction.

The water use estimates set off alarm bells for the residents. Chile had already been in an unprecedented drought since 2010. By 2021, more than half the country’s 19 million residents lived in areas experiencing severe water scarcity, forcing hundreds of rural communities to rely on tankers to deliver drinking water.

The local activists ultimately built the case against one of the largest companies on the planet. After months of meetings and advocacy to spread awareness, they were able to put a referendum question to the residents of Cerrillos about the project in December 2019. The results were damning: 49% of voters chose to reject the project, while 38% wanted it to go forward.

After both the municipality and community members filed claims against Google in 2020, the company returned with a new proposal in February 2022. It offered to cool the data center exclusively with air-conditioning rather than with water.

Across the city in Quilicura, opposition was building too. Microsoft announced its intention to build a data center in the community in 2022, the same year strict water-rationing rules had come into effect in Santiago. As in Cerrillos, residents were worried that another large data center would threaten their access to water and provide little in return.

analysis.tldr: Big tech companies are facing local resistance worldwide for using massive amounts of drinking water to cool AI servers, which could eventually push them to build expensive alternative cooling systems or rethink where they set up shop.
the_story: A University of California paper in April 2023 estimated that training the original ChatGPT required 185,000 gallons of water, with every extended conversation using about a bottle's worth.
A single hyperscale data center can consume between 1 million and 5 million gallons of water a day, rivaling the daily use of a city of up to 50,000 people.
Data centers require clean water to avoid damaging equipment, leading them to tap into public drinking water sources and compete directly with local communities.

In Santiago, Chile, local residents formed groups like MOSACAT and successfully pushed back against a $200 million Google data center project that planned to use 169 liters of water per second from a restricted underground aquifer.
Faced with community opposition and legal challenges, Google eventually revised its proposal in February 2022 to cool its Santiago data center using air-conditioning instead of water.
analysis.what_happened: Tech companies are rushing to build massive data centers packed with specialized computer chips (GPUs) to power artificial intelligence. These chips generate extreme heat and require millions of gallons of water daily to stay cool, sparking global pushback from local communities worried about water shortages.
analysis.analogy: It is like someone setting up a massive, thirsty factory in the middle of a drought-hit neighborhood and using up all the water from the local tap to run their machinery.
why_it_matters_india: Global tech giants are investing heavily in Indian data centers to capture the country's booming digital market.
India already faces severe water stress in many urban and rural areas where data centers are being planned.
Local resistance and stricter environmental rules could force tech companies to spend more money on alternative cooling technologies.
Higher infrastructure and cooling costs for companies like Microsoft and Google could ripple into the broader costs of digital and cloud services.

impacts.target: Global tech stocks like Microsoft & Alphabet
impacts.rationale: Stricter regulations, delays, and redesign costs for data centers can temporarily squeeze profit margins, though these are massive global giants.

impacts.target: India's real estate & data center infrastructure sector
impacts.rationale: Growing demand for data storage in India means more construction, but future projects may face tighter local scrutiny over natural resources.

events.headline: WTO members conclude review of US import surcharges following removal of measure

items.title: WTO members conclude review of US import surcharges following removal of measure
items.summary: WTO members have concluded the consultations regarding the 10% import surcharge adopted by the United States.

events.article_text:
This note has been prepared by the WTO Secretariat to assist public understanding about the work of the WTO's councils, committees and other bodies. It is not intended as a complete account of all issues raised at the meeting. These can be found in the formal meeting minutes.

At a meeting on 2 October, the WTO's Committee on Balance of Payments resumed consultations with the United States regarding its 10% import surcharge.

Members noted that the US measure was terminated on 24 July, thereby concluding the consultations. Members then finalized the consultation report, which was adopted ad referendum on 12 October. The report will now be submitted to the General Council for review.

The United States earlier notified the Committee that, on 20 February, an import surcharge of 10% ad valorem was being imposed on imports of goods from all trading partners, subject to certain product exceptions, pursuant to Section 122 of the US Trade Act of 1974. The United States cited fundamental international payment problems as the justification for the import surcharge. The measure was due to be terminated on 24 July unless the US Congress agreed to extend it.

Following the notification of the temporary import surcharge to the Committee, several members requested consultations with the United States. These consultations took place during a 5 May meeting of the Committee, where the discussion centred on the US balance of payment situation, as well as the necessity, design and application of the import surcharge.

WTO members facing balance-of-payment difficulty may apply import restrictions under provisions in the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) 1994 and the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS).

The Committee on Balance-of-Payments Restrictions consults with WTO members who maintain import restrictions for balance-of-payments reasons. The International Monetary Fund participates in the consultations by providing a statement on the consulting member's balance-of-payments situation and external reserve position.

Problems viewing this page? If so, please contact [email protected] giving details of the operating system and web browser you are using.

analysis.tldr: The removal of a US 10 percent tax on imports removes a hurdle for global trade, which helps Indian companies exporting goods to America.
the_story: At a meeting on 2 October, the WTO's (World Trade Organization - a global group that handles rules of trade between nations) Committee on Balance of Payments concluded talks with the United States.
The US had earlier imposed a 10 percent import surcharge (an extra tax on imported goods) on all trading partners starting 20 February, citing payment problems.
Members noted that this US measure was officially terminated on 24 July, ending the need for further consultations.
analysis.what_happened: The US ended a temporary 10 percent tax it had placed on goods coming from other countries back in February. Because the US removed this tax on 24 July, global trade officials at the World Trade Organization formally wrapped up their review of the matter in October.
analysis.analogy: It is like a local market temporarily charging an extra fee on all outside vendors, and then dropping the fee so everyone can go back to trading normally.
why_it_matters_india: The US dropped its 10 percent import tax, removing an extra cost for foreign goods entering America.
Indian companies that sell goods to the US no longer face this specific surcharge.
Lower costs for selling to the US can help improve business for Indian exporters.
Smoother global trade reduces overall market friction, which is generally positive for international business confidence.

impacts.target: Indian export businesses (like textiles and engineering goods)
impacts.rationale: Removing the US import tax makes Indian goods cheaper for American buyers, which is good for Indian company revenues.
Better global trade rules are generally welcomed by stock markets, creating a mild positive mood for investors.

watch_next: Any future announcements from the US regarding new trade rules or import taxes
Reports from the WTO General Council after they review this finalized report
analysis.caveats: This report only deals with the formal wrap-up of a past US tax that has already been ended, so the immediate economic relief happened back in July.

history.title: The crisis that taught Asia to hoard dollars
history.what: Thailand ran out of reserves defending its currency peg and let the baht float. It fell 50% in months. The panic spread through Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia within weeks, becoming the worst emerging market crisis of the era.
history.why: These economies had borrowed heavily in dollars while earning in local currency — a mismatch that is invisible while the exchange rate is fixed and fatal the moment it moves. Their central banks had promised stable pegs, which encouraged still more dollar borrowing. When growth slowed and the dollar strengthened, speculators tested the pegs and the reserves ran out.
history.impact: Indonesia's economy shrank 13% in a year and its government fell. South Korea, a developed economy, needed the largest IMF bailout in history to that point. Millions fell back into poverty. Asian shares lost 60-80% in dollar terms.
history.policy: IMF bailouts with severe conditions, which remain bitterly resented in the region. More durably, the affected countries abandoned rigid pegs, let their currencies float, and began accumulating enormous foreign exchange reserves as self-insurance so they would never have to ask again.
history.consequence: Asia's reserve hoard is the direct descendant of 1997. Those reserves were recycled into US government bonds, which helped hold global interest rates down for two decades — one of the quiet forces behind the cheap money of the 2000s, and therefore behind the housing bubble that followed.
history.pattern: Borrowing in a currency you do not earn is the most reliable way to turn a slowdown into a collapse. It is invisible in good times and decisive in bad ones. Check what currency a country, a company or a project owes in.
history.india_echo: India was barely touched, because the capital account was still largely closed and the rupee was not freely convertible. The lesson Indian policymakers drew — open up slowly, keep reserves large — still shapes RBI policy today, and explains why India has weathered every emerging market scare since with discomfort rather than disaster.
history.watch_for: Countries with large dollar debts, thin reserves and a currency the central bank insists is stable. The combination is the setup, every time.
